title: Opioid Overdose & Naloxone
summary: Unresponsive with slow or no breathing after drug use: call {EMERGENCY}, give breaths or CPR, and give naloxone as soon as it is available.

callEmergency.headline: Call {EMERGENCY} for any suspected overdose
when: Unresponsive or can't be woken, or slow, shallow or no breathing
Blue or grey lips or fingertips
Even if naloxone has worked – it can wear off before the drug does

steps.title: Check for response
steps.text: Shout their name and rub firmly on the breastbone. If no response, call {EMERGENCY} and put the phone on speaker.

steps.title: Open the airway and check breathing
steps.text: If not breathing normally, start CPR (or rescue breaths if you are trained and a pulse is present).

steps.title: Give naloxone
steps.text: Give naloxone as soon as it is available, following the instructions on the kit (nasal spray or injection into the thigh or upper arm). Keep giving breaths or CPR in between.

steps.title: Give another dose if needed
steps.text: If they are not breathing normally after a few minutes, give another dose if available, following the kit instructions.

steps.title: When they are breathing
steps.text: Place them in the recovery position and stay with them. They may wake suddenly and be confused or in withdrawal.

steps.title: Stay until help arrives
steps.text: Naloxone can wear off before the opioid, so they can stop breathing again. Watch breathing continuously.
points: BC Centre for Disease Control (Toward the Heart) teaches SAVE ME: Stimulate, Airway, Ventilate, Evaluate, Muscular injection (naloxone), Evaluate & support
In Canada, the Good Samaritan Drug Overdose Act gives some legal protection to people who call 911 at an overdose

doNot: Do not put them in a cold bath or try to make them vomit
Do not assume one dose of naloxone is enough
